passage:
Sahil: you don't get it!!
Keerthana: I DO get it, you promised you'd come
Sahil: I said maybe
Keerthana: you said yes 😠
Sahil: STOP SHOUTING
Keerthana: I'm not shouting, I'm typing in capitals because I'm so hurt
Sahil: ...
Keerthana: ok that came out louder than I meant. can we take ten minutes and then talk properly?
Sahil: yes
Sahil: I'm sorry I said maybe when I meant no
Sahil: I didn't want to say no to your face
Keerthana: thanks for saying it. I'd rather hear a no than get a maybe. I wanted you there. that's really all it was 🙂

qa.q: What did Keerthana say Sahil had promised?
qa.a: Keerthana said Sahil had promised to come.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling behind the capitals and anger?
qa.a: Keerthana was hurt and wanted Sahil there, and said that was all it was. The later softer tone shows the anger came from hurt.

qa.q: What worked when Keerthana changed approach?
qa.a: Keerthana noticed it came out too loud, asked for a short break and suggested talking properly. Taking a break and lowering the voice worked better than escalating.

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt when Keerthana yelled?
qa.a: Sahil probably felt attacked and defensive, which is why Sahil told Keerthana to stop shouting. Sahil later apologised for saying maybe.

grounding: A teenager yells in a quarrel from hurt, then takes a break and returns to talk more calmly.

passage: The bus to the fair at Kasba was late, and Nikita's brother Gautam had left without her again. She stormed into the courtyard. "You always do this!" she yelled. Gautam yelled back, "You're never ready!" Their grandmother looked out from the kitchen. Nikita's chest burned. She stopped, pressed her lips together, and walked to the well. She splashed water on her face, breathed slowly, and lowered her shoulders. When she came back, she said in a quieter voice, "I was really upset. I wanted to go with you." Gautam blinked. "I didn't know that. Next time I'll wait."

qa.q: Who looked out from the kitchen during the yelling?
qa.a: Their grandmother looked out from the kitchen.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when she yelled at Gautam?
qa.a: She was hurt and frustrated at being left behind, and wanted to be heard. She later said she really wanted to go with him.

qa.q: What could Nikita and Gautam do the next time a quarrel starts?
qa.a: Take a break, lower their voices and come back to talk, as Nikita did. That works better than yelling back.

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt when Nikita came back quieter?
qa.a: He seemed surprised and softened, since he hadn't known she wanted to go with him. He promised to wait.

grounding: A teenager yells from hurt in a quarrel, takes a break, lowers the voice and returns to talk.

passage:
In their Nairobi flat, Zanele's voice got louder and louder. "You never let me go anywhere! Everyone else is going to Amani's party!"
Her mother Wanjiru's voice rose too. "Because it ends at midnight and nobody's parents will be there!"
"You don't trust me!" Zanele was shouting now, her throat raw. "You never listen!"
She stopped. Her hands were shaking. This was going nowhere.
"I need a break," she said, much quieter, and walked out to the balcony. She stood there breathing in the cool air, watching the matatus below.
Ten minutes later, she went back in. Her mother was sitting at the table. Zanele sat opposite. "Can we talk without shouting? I just want you to hear why it matters to me."
Wanjiru nodded slowly. "I'm listening."

qa.q: Where did Zanele go to take a break?
qa.a: Out to the balcony.

qa.q: What was Zanele feeling while she shouted?
qa.a: Zanele felt frustrated and hurt, wanting her mother to hear her and trust her.

qa.q: Which choice of Zanele's worked, and why?
qa.a: Taking a break on the balcony and coming back to talk in a lower voice worked, because it stopped the argument escalating and got her mother listening.

qa.q: How might Wanjiru have felt when Zanele came back calmly?
qa.a: Wanjiru probably felt relieved and more willing to listen, since the shouting had stopped.

grounding: A teenager yells in a quarrel with her mother, then takes a break and returns to talk quietly, which works better.

passage:
At the school council meeting, Samir and Trisha were arguing about the annual day budget. It started calm, but soon they were both shouting across the table.
"You always take the sports side!" Trisha yelled.
"And you only care about the dance!" Samir shouted back.
Other members went quiet. The teacher in charge, Mr Kulkarni, raised a hand. "Let's take a five-minute break."
Samir walked out to the corridor and leaned against the wall, breathing hard. Trisha stayed in the room, arms crossed.
When they came back, Samir spoke first, quietly. "Sorry. I got loud. Can we split it and try both?"
Trisha let out a breath. "Okay. I was loud too."
They worked it out in fifteen minutes.

qa.q: How long a break did Mr Kulkarni call?
qa.a: A five-minute break.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when he shouted across the table?
qa.a: Samir felt frustrated and unheard, believing Trisha only cared about the dance.

qa.q: How did the break help the argument?
qa.a: It gave both of them time to calm down, so they could return with lower voices and find a compromise.

qa.q: How might the other members have felt during the shouting?
qa.a: They probably felt uncomfortable and tense, which is why they went quiet.

grounding: At a school council meeting, two teenagers shout, take a break, and return to talk calmly, finding a solution.

passage:
Dear Ayesha,
I'm sorry for yelling at you yesterday in the library. When you said my part of the project was "not good enough," I got so angry I raised my voice. Everyone turned and looked at us.
I think I was hurt more than angry. I'd worked on it all weekend, and I wanted you to see that.
Shouting didn't make you understand. It just made us both upset. I should have said, "I need a minute," gone outside, and come back to talk.
Can we meet after school and go through it calmly? I'll listen to what you think needs fixing if you'll listen to why I did it that way.
Pradeep

qa.q: Where did Pradeep yell at Ayesha?
qa.a: In the library.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when raising the voice?
qa.a: Pradeep felt hurt and angry, wanting Ayesha to see how much work had gone into the project.

qa.q: What would Pradeep do differently next time?
qa.a: Pradeep would say "I need a minute", step outside, and come back to talk calmly instead of shouting.

qa.q: If you were Ayesha, how might this letter feel?
qa.a: You might feel relieved and more willing to listen, since Pradeep apologised and asked to talk calmly.

grounding: In a letter, a teenager apologises for yelling in a quarrel and plans to take a break and return to talk.

passage: Lavanya, you heard the shouting from your balcony last night, didn't you? Yeah. That was me, Kiran, at full volume. Papa said I can't apply to the hostel school in Dehradun, and before he'd even finished I was yelling, "You never let me do anything!" He shouted back, and it got so loud Amma shut the windows. I wasn't only angry. I was hurt, because I'd shown him the brochure three times and he'd never read it. Then I did something new. I said, "I need ten minutes," and went up to the terrace. I counted the water tanks on every roof. When I came down, my voice was normal. I said, "I want you to read the brochure before you decide." He read it. He still said no, for now. But this time he actually heard me.

qa.q: Where is the hostel school Kiran wanted to apply to?
qa.a: In Dehradun.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling while yelling at Papa?
qa.a: Kiran was angry but mostly hurt, because Papa had never read the brochure despite being shown it three times.

qa.q: What worked better than the shouting?
qa.a: Taking a ten-minute break, then coming back with a normal voice and a clear request: read the brochure before deciding.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when Kiran came down speaking normally?
qa.a: Papa probably felt calmer and more able to listen, which is why he read the brochure, even though he still said no for now.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager yelling at a parent out of hurt and a wish to be heard, then taking a break and returning with a lower voice.
